chunk_findings.detail: `_prior_memory_events` returns every prior `memory.recorded` event for the memory, including events already redacted by earlier re-records, and the loop does not consult `st.redacted_memory_events` or the second return value of `redact_event_text` before emitting the audit event. Given a memory added once, then re-recorded twice, the original event’s text is already `SUPERSEDED_MARKER` on the second re-record, but the code still calls `redact_event_text` on it and appends another `memory.redacted` event referencing the same prior event. This produces duplicate/false audit records and makes repeated re-records grow the log quadratically (after N re-records, the first event has N-1 redaction audits). The loop should skip ids already in `st.redacted_memory_events`, or only append `memory.redacted` when an actual redaction occurred.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/memory.py:72-81

chunk_findings.detail: `_rewrite_line` replaces the shard by creating a new temporary file (`shard.name + ".redact"`) with `write_text` and then `os.replace`ing it over the shard. On POSIX, the replacement file inherits the temporary file’s mode/owner, not the original shard’s. Given a shard that was created with a restrictive mode (for example `0600`) or non-default permissions, a successful `redact_event_text` call silently changes the shard to the process default mode (often `0644`) and may change ownership, so other local users can now read the remaining event log contents. This is a security regression in a change whose purpose is to reduce exposure of sensitive log data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:_rewrite_line

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test checks the `memory.redacted` marker’s `subject` and `data.reason`, but it never checks the required `data.event` field. The new fixture in `tests/fixtures/event_kinds.json` and the coherence exemption both describe this event as naming the superseded event id; if the handler emits `memory.redacted` with `event` set to the new event id, the memory id, an empty string, or another wrong value, the test still passes. Thus the test does not enforce the audit link that the redaction marker refers to the prior `memory.recorded` event.

chunk_findings.detail: The permission fix does not remove the temporary exposure window. `_rewrite_line` still creates the replacement file (`shard.name + ".redact"`) with `write_text`, which uses the process umask (commonly producing mode `0644`), writes a full copy of the shard into it, and only then chmods it to the original shard mode. Given a shard created as `0600` and containing private event text, a crash or kill between `write_text` and `os.chmod`/`os.replace` leaves a world-readable `*.redact` file in the events directory; even without a crash, that file is readable during the write/chmod window if the directory permits traversal. The probe “a 0600 shard stays 0600 after redact_event_text” only checks the final shard mode, not the mode of the temporary copy or the crash path. The temp file should be created with the intended restrictive mode from the start (e.g. `os.open(..., mode=original_mode & 0o7777)` or a private `mkstemp`), not made world-readable and chmodded afterward.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:_rewrite_line

chunk_findings.detail: The redaction and its audit are not atomic, and the marker-based skip can make a lost audit permanent. `log.redact_event_text` replaces the prior event line immediately (via `_rewrite_line`’s `os.replace`), then the code appends the `memory.redacted` audit event as a separate log append. If the append fails or the process dies after the file replacement but before the audit is committed, the prior event text is already `[REDACTED:superseded]` while no `memory.redacted` event exists and `st.redacted_memory_events` does not contain the event id. On the next re-record, line 79 skips any prior event whose text equals `SUPERSEDED_MARKER` without checking `st.redacted_memory_events` or the presence of the audit event, so the missing audit is never retried. Concrete failure: memory `M` has one prior recorded event; during re-record, `redact_event_text` succeeds, then `log.append("memory.redacted", ...)` raises (disk full) or the process is killed. The event log now contains the marker but no audit; a subsequent `memory add --id M` sees the marker and skips, leaving an unaudited redaction contrary to [D-event-log-redaction-forward].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/memory.py:72-81

chunk_findings.detail: The permission-preservation fix is incomplete and can still leak or corrupt data. `tmp = shard.with_name(shard.name + ".redact")` is a predictable name, and `tmp.write_text(...)` creates/opens it with the process default mode and follows symlinks. Given a shard with mode `0600` in a directory readable by other users and a normal umask such as `022`, the replacement file is created `0644` and contains the whole rewritten shard before `os.chmod` runs, so other local users can read all other events during the redaction. If the shard directory is writable by another local user, that user can pre-create `shard.jsonl.redact` as a symlink to an arbitrary writable file; `write_text` then truncates/overwrites that target, and `os.chmod`/`os.chown` follow the symlink as well. The code should create a unique, exclusive temp file with the desired mode before writing content.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:_rewrite_line

chunk_findings.detail: The audit-link assertion still does not prove that `memory.redacted.data.event` names the superseded `memory.recorded` event. It only checks that the value is non-empty, is present in `state.redacted_memory_events`, and differs from the correction event id. A buggy implementation could emit the redaction marker with `data.event` set to the marker event’s own id and append that same id to `state.redacted_memory_events`; the test would still pass because `superseded` is non-empty, is in the set, and is not the correction event id, while the prior memory event’s id is never recorded as redacted. The test should compare `superseded` against the id of the prior `memory.recorded` event whose text is now `[REDACTED:superseded]` (for example `recorded[0]["id"]`) rather than relying only on membership in state.

chunk_findings.detail: The re-record path now only appends a `memory.redacted` tombstone event; it does not redact, replace, or doctor-flag the prior `memory.recorded` event. Given `ddflow memory add --id M1da6c78dd8 "server at [REDACTED:ipv4]"` followed by `ddflow memory add --id M1da6c78dd8 "server at private"`, the first event line containing `text: "server at [REDACTED:ipv4]"` remains in `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl` and in backups/git. The new `memory.redacted` event only names `prior.id`; any raw log reader, backup tool, or consumer that does not implement tombstone filtering still sees the private address. Since this diff contains no in-place redaction and no doctor check for unredacted superseded addresses, the reported bug (private text remains committed in the event log) is still reproducible.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/memory.py:80

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test no longer verifies the stated privacy bug. It records `old stale fact [REDACTED:ipv4]`, re-records it, and then checks only that the current memory state text is corrected and that one `memory.redacted` audit event names the old event. It does not check that the prior event’s text is redacted, removed, or flagged anywhere in `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl`. With the append-only tombstone behavior reflected by the removal of the in-place rewrite/redaction helpers, the original `memory.recorded` event remains in the event log with `data.text` containing `[REDACTED:ipv4]`. The test passes while the private address is still committed in the raw event log, which is exactly the reported bug; the stated expected outcome was redaction of the prior event when it carries an address, or a doctor flag, and neither is asserted or present in the changed files.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_memory.py:test_re_recording_tombstones_the_superseded_text

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to prove that duplicate redaction audits are not stacked, but it only asserts `len(redacted) == 2`. It does not assert that the two audits refer to two distinct superseded event ids. For example, a buggy implementation that appends a `memory.redacted` audit for the first recorded event on every re-record, while never auditing the second superseded event, would still produce two `memory.redacted` events and pass this test. That contradicts the test’s comment that `e1` is tombstoned at the second record and `e2` at the third, and it would leave a duplicate audit for `e1` plus no tombstone for `e2`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new re-record path performs the in-place redaction (`log.redact_event_text`, which is implemented via `_rewrite_line`/file replacement according to the manifest) before the `memory.redacted` audit event is appended, and the surrounding `log.transaction()` cannot roll back that filesystem replacement. If the transaction aborts after line 80 returns—for example `DD.after_add` raises, or the process is killed before the audit append at lines 81-85 is committed—the prior `memory.recorded` event line has already been replaced with `[REDACTED:superseded]`, but no `memory.redacted` event exists. On replay, `st.redacted_memory_events` will not contain the prior event id, so the redaction is unaudited; if the transaction buffers appends, the new `memory.recorded` event can also be lost, leaving the old memory text destroyed without either an audit event or a committed correction. This contradicts the code comment that each redaction is audited and breaks the atomicity promised by `log.transaction()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/memory.py:80-85

chunk_findings.detail: The redaction API keeps a content-addressed commitment to the superseded private text. `redact_event_text` proves that the event id is a function of the event data by recomputing the id after replacing `data[field]`; the documented caller then appends a `memory.redacted` event whose `data.event` is `original.id`. Given a prior `memory.recorded` event with text `server at [REDACTED:ipv4]`, after re-record the raw string is gone from the original line, but the new `memory.redacted` line still contains the original event’s content-addressed id. That id is a deterministic hash of the original event, including the private address; for a low-entropy LAN address an attacker can enumerate plausible addresses and verify them against the retained id, so the address remains recoverable from `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl`. The earlier refutation only checked that the raw address string was absent; it does not address the retained content-addressed id.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:redact_event_text

chunk_findings.detail: The exception path leaks the file descriptor returned by `tempfile.mkstemp`. `fd` is obtained before the `try`, and `os.fdopen(fd, ...)` only takes ownership later. If `shard.stat()` or `os.chmod(fd, ...)` raises before `os.fdopen` is called—for example, the shard is deleted between `read_text()` and `stat()`, or `fchmod` fails on a filesystem that does not support it—the `except BaseException` block unlinks `tmp` but never closes `fd`. Each such failed rewrite leaks a file descriptor.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:_rewrite_line

chunk_findings.detail: The skip condition `if prior.id in st.redacted_memory_events: continue` treats the presence of a `memory.redacted` audit event as proof that the prior `memory.recorded` event’s text was actually redacted. It is not: `st.redacted_memory_events` is populated solely by the `memory.redacted` handler, so any log that contains a `memory.redacted` event whose prior event line was not rewritten—e.g. the tombstone-only behavior from the intermediate commit mentioned in the triage, or any future path that emits the audit without a successful redaction—will poison this skip. Given a prior event `E` with `text: "server at [REDACTED:ipv4]"` and a `memory.redacted` event naming `E`, a later `memory add --id M... "server at private"` computes `prior_events`, sees `E.id in st.redacted_memory_events`, skips `E`, and leaves the address in `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl`. The guard must also verify that the prior event’s text is actually `SUPERSEDED_MARKER` (or otherwise confirm redaction) before skipping.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/memory.py:76

chunk_findings.detail: `redact_event_text` recomputes the event’s content address and rewrites the line, so the original event id no longer exists in the shard. The docstring tells the caller to append a `memory.redacted` audit event naming `original.id`, and the prior review’s test asserts that `data.event` is the superseded event’s id. Given a recorded event with id `X`, after `redact_event_text(X, "text", marker)` the log contains a line with a new id `Y`, not `X`; the audit event then points to `X`, which is absent, and nowhere records `Y`. Any consumer that resolves the audit’s event reference, or tries to verify that the marked line is the redacted successor of `X`, cannot do so. The method has the new id in `redacted` but the documented audit path leaves the log with a dangling reference and no link from the audit to the redacted event.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:redact_event_text

chunk_findings.detail: `_rewrite_line` replaces the shard with a newly created file but copies only the mode bits. `tempfile.mkstemp` creates the replacement file with the process’s effective owner and group, and `os.replace` makes that the shard’s owner/group. For example, if the shard is `0640 alice:ddflow` and the redaction is performed by a process with effective group `alice` (or by root), the redacted shard becomes `0640 alice:alice` (or `0600 root:root`). The intended `ddflow` group can lose access, users in the process’s group can gain access, and a root-run doctor can make a user-owned `0600` log unreadable by its owner. A privacy redaction path that rewrites a restrictive shard should preserve ownership/ACL/xattrs, not just mode.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py:_rewrite_line
